item.title: The Fun Factor
item.description:
Given our reputation, it might surprise you to learn that LessWrong loves fun posts! We also appreciates rigor and, especially in end-of-year reviews, technical depth. Sometimes, our authors seem to get stuck in droughts: long stretches of low-karma posts, typically un-fun, un-rigorous, and a bit technical. You might think these doldrums are the prelude to an impressive, well-received synthesis, but they're not. They just go on and on. When authors break through a drought with a great post, it's usually with a fun, personal, tangible, funny narrative or advice.

I hit on this framing after I spent the weekend using Claude Code to analyze the LessWrong corpus looking for patterns in what makes for a great post. Surface features of language and topic explain only a little of the variance in karma. The author's identity explains quite a bit more.

One of my main findings is that LessWrong shifted away from its early preference for dense technical topics, philosophy, statistics, and study advice, and has come to award higher karma in recent years to articles on health and disease, X-risk, and, of course, AI.

Using these surface attributes, I could only explain about half the reception any given post gets. It was a little discouraging to find that in general, authors mostly don't improve with experience, except perhaps the most prolific[1].

But as I reflected on the results and re-read some great LessWrong articles, I felt like the real core of what LessWrong seems to love are fun, personal, tangible posts, not just rigorous technical prose.

My suspicion is that we under-encourage our authors to write fun posts and include personal narrative in their work, perhaps because it feels a bit counter to LessWrong's rationalist ethos. But it's an important aspect of what we actually reward on this site, even in end-of-year reviews, and of what's associated with authors breaking through a drought.

Go forth! Write fun posts! Quirky posts! Give us advice! Tell us a story about your life! Teach us something you know! You don't have to solve a big impressive problem. You can write about Microwave Cooking for One! You can analyze sentence lengths throughout history!

And to the great authors on this site: please give us some writing advice on how you make your posts fun. What's your writing process? Do you have to be in a good mood? Are you just having fun all the time when you write, or do you have to work hard to put the fun into your prose? Serious thinkers want to know!

Illustrative breakthrough posts and non-breakthrough great posts

"Review" is the final Review score from high-karma voters. Posts from 2025 onward have not been reviewed yet, and "—" means the post never received a final score. A "primary" post is the kind of content people come to LessWrong to read, and excludes "secondary" posts which are things like admin posts and brief questions to the community.

A breakthrough is an author's first great post after at least 8 primary posts and at least 12 months without one. A great post has inflation-adjusted karma at or above the bottom 5% of curated posts.

item.title: Heroism in AI Safety
item.description:
What role do heroes have in AI safety?

This blog post was written in my personal capacity and free time. Gemini 4 Neon and Opus 5.5 assisted in ideating and writing up rebuttals for initial drafts.

In Gentleness and the Artificial Other, Joe Carlsmith brings up Timothy Treadwell—the subject of the documentary Grizzly Man.Timothy Treadwell was a man who loved bears: he was gentle with them, filming them up close, hanging out with them, even refusing to set up electric fences around his camp or to carry around bear mace. He did this for 13 years. Then he was eaten by a bear.

Looking into the eyes of one of Timothy Treadwell’s bears, Herzog famously observes “no kinship, no understanding, no mercy,” only nature, indifferent.

In AI safety, we have internalised this warning quite deeply. Looking at the prospect of misaligned artificial superintelligence, it can feel like only a mailed fist would suit these hands, the only responsible posture wariness, the only honest recourse violence. Indeed, Carlsmith’s essay is an argument for learning the “art of both”—holding, clinging onto wonder and openness toward the artificial Other without forgetting that we might still get eaten. It is important to both appreciate the stardust, comets, constellations in the inky maw, but also that we are indeed putting our head between its jaws.

If you convince yourself you are standing in the path of an indifferent predator, there is a very specific dynamic which emerges, which I will refer to as heroism. Consider the language of “wartime” and “no adults in the room” and “great writers” and “ten people on the inside.” Consider a lone researcher pulling 2 a.m. shifts on an evals suite because if I miss this, nobody will catch it, the mania of attending to the Claudes just one more time before you go to bed. Consider still the intoxication of a small few, only a thousandish brave souls in the know (high-context), holding back the abyss, not one iota eastward.

Here, I will resist being legible (sorry!), and like with the frame of war mode, we all kind of know what it means, with slightly to moderately different perspectives, which I don’t want to pin down but wish to leave a point of active discussion and confusion. Some more concrete examples:

  • In Eliezer Yudkowsky’s Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality, a core doctrine is heroic responsibility: if something very bad is coming, you can’t just shrug and abdicate responsibility to the adults. Rather, the outcome is yours to secure. I think this is quite a noble impulse (a big reason this field exists at all), but also indelibly bakes a fantasy-quest grammar into the DNA of AI safety.
  • In Sebastian Mallaby’s biography The Infinity Machine, a recurring tension is Hassabis as the pure scientist versus Hassabis as Ender Wiggin from Ender’s Game. Like Ender, Hassabis is a child prodigy raised on tournaments, sometimes ostracized by peers, driven by a deep need to do the most important thing. When the race heats up, the heroic frame makes clear its livid justification: someone will cross the Rubicon, so it had better be me.
  • And of course, there is Jacob Coxon, who, when he resigned from Anthropic from a park bench in Alamo Square and posted that the people building AI earnestly believe it could kill us all, it was individual, costly, decisive. Within 36 hours, it had over 150 million views and caused a preference cascade across mainstream media. Yet also the aftermath, such as the whiplash when he joked about his OpenAI equity at Stanford (“I like money, bro”), got dragged across social media, reversed course to pledge it all away, and admitted the media storm was taking a toll.

If you take these together, I think one thing to understand is that “Is heroism good or bad?” is a hard question to pose. Variously it is taking ownership, but also a way to confer status, commitment to wartime, a means to rouse morale. I feel the best way to think of it is as a subconscious disposition. No one is writing down in fellowship applications that they want to be a hero, or putting it on their personal website, but it primes your gut reaction in a certain way.

So, is heroism good or bad?

Pros

  • Heroism enables people to do ambitious things. One thing that we should credit it for is defeating the diffusion of responsibility: many years ago, no institution was assigned the problem of aligning superintelligence, yet work began because a handful of people saw a gap to fill anyways. It seems likely that without their conceptual thinking we would be several years behind. Even now, heroic ethos gives people license to attempt massive, weird things without waiting for credential or committee, taking large, ambitious research bets. It’s possible and likely that there is no “normal” or “institutional” path to aligning ASI, and we must strike out ambitiously to succeed.
  • Heroism is a good rallying cry. In extraordinary times, it is how war mode pays its people. Feedback loops in research are years long, and most people are afraid to “call their shot”. It’s hard to remain confident without motivation in this way. It also creates fast trust; strangers who share a wartime story can quickly assume good faith in one another’s motives. This is also good for commitment: ideally, building a public identity around preventing catastrophe should act as a moral anchor to enrage the public if you renege on your moral commitments.
  • Heroism fuels courage. Publishing an unpleasant result, walking away from equity, all of these are in fact hard! In bonafide emergencies, in crunch time, in the final hour, we will still need people willing to step into the breach.

Cons

  • Heroism can be deeply unhealthy. This is pretty obvious: the stakes are astronomical, so it can be hard to not devote every waking hour to the great cause.
  • Heroism is just not a great way to make something reliably safe. If we take systems safety fields like aviation and nuclear power as examples, they didn’t become safe by recruiting the bravest pilots and operators. Rather, they became safe through redundancy, incident reporting, systems explicitly designed to reduce cases where someone has to step up and be the hero. One-off bursts of heroism aren’t reliable, and we’ll fail in the long run if we rely too heavily on them.
  • Heroism as an aesthetic is innately oppositional, which locks you out of certain modes of thinking. A hero needs a foil, a dragon, a villain, a messy government institution to work around. Once you clench the mailed fist, it clenches back, tightening something deep inside you that activates this atavistic sense of tribalism. It closes off some important aspect of collaborative, curious, and incremental thinking that we might also need to solve big problems.
    • Note: To be clear, I’m not claiming that we should or shouldn’t do a certain thing here, probably shame is useful and warranted as a tool in some cases. But it seems bad to lock off one frame of thinking for yourself.
  • Heroism is fundamentally optimistic in the goodness of you and your allies. But sometimes there is also a need to be cynical, to doubt people who might try to take advantage of you, or to think that you aren’t as strong willed as you hope you might be.

OK, it seems clear to me that some heroism is necessary. We do need big, radical bets, which have crazy, nutty research leads. But it’s also flawed in some deep ways. We need to run the adventurer’s party in a way with staying power.

So what I’m really trying to say is: do the good thing and try to work hard as a culture to not do the bad thing. What this could mean is:

  • Guard against the unsavoury aspects of heroism. One thing I’ve observed, with the increase of attention, resources, and importance in AI safety is a moderate increase in NBA-like celebrity culture. Here heroism kind of curdles into fandom (or as Gemini 4 Neon says, “status architecture”), like podcasts, Twitter threads, hushed debates over the GOAT or whatever. Competitive debate, IMO, is instructive here. It’s a high-context intellectual culture which regularly suffers from entrenched celebrity dynamics, with social corruption, social climbing, hero worship. Significant effort has to be put into making sure a debate organisation is welcoming, curating a culture and orienting towards a shared goal, but still able to get things done. In AI safety, it’d be even worse: unlike basketball or a debate tournament, there isn’t even a good scoreboard! And, the fans are causal. Attention moves funding, hiring, and mentees. We should be quite suspicious if our manner of speaking starts sounding like an ESPN segment or The Deep 3.
  • Show your thinking and your failures. There is some truth that research leads matter a lot. They have good taste which is illegible to junior researchers in an ill-defined way, and tend to make good judgements in terms of your research choices. So it can be easy to try to distill as best as you can. But as Dan Murfet once pointed out to me, if you try to distill from particular people, you only ever capture the surface things. The reality of research is mostly embarrassing, with many false starts and confusing results (you usually only see that inside a PhD, when an advisor lets you see the sausage factory). Hero worship raises the price of looking confused in public, which hides the process, and if we want to actually transmit research taste, we’ll want researchers to post dead ends, the half-formed notes, failures.
    • Specifically, mentor, reach out. War mode whispers that there is no time for slow apprenticeship: you need to be shipping yesterday! That’s a great way to guarantee we run out of the exact senior leads we are bottlenecked by. We must believe in the ability of people to be good before they are good, taking the time to accept that some of your best work may not be with you as first author. In this way, I think it’s good to take mentorship seriously: spend time to expose your reasoning traces and your latents, to talk through their theory of change, to be invested in their success and commiserate in their failure.
    • Note: I really take “Teacher for a day, father for a lifetime” seriously!
  • Reduce status hierarchy. I don’t like how we sometimes talk of roles as research and non-research, or technical and non-technical. Doing engineering work to maintain an evals pipeline, or managing a research org, or building compute infrastructure, or navigating policy are all mission-critical, heroic too. You’re not a porter or supporting cast! These all also have their own steep learning curves, their own hard-won taste, and their own forms of courage. There’s a natural tendency for an intellectual culture to afford status to those who cultivate intellect in a legible way, but we want to get ambitious alignment done, not just ambitious research, of which research is only a subset of the activities.

In the end, this brings us back to Carlsmith’s bear, and the art of both.

We do not need to give up the mailed fist. There are sharp teeth in the dark, and there will be moments, crises of nerve, where bonafide, costly heroism is the only thing that saves us. But we need to remember that the velvet glove exists too, and we have two hands! 

A mailed fist is a terrible hand to build with. If we never take the gauntlet off, we lose the qualities required of us as a community and culture: a softness to admit when an agenda is a dead end, a kindness to show a junior researcher how to be a senior researcher, and a humility to be one among many. We want to write constitutions which encode thick notions of alignment: legitimate, representative, and compassionate. We may need to make deals with AIs, to be as trustworthy and earnest as they believe us to be, to comport ourselves with gentleness. We need the mailed fist for the bear—and the velvet glove for each other!

item.title: The Disappointment of a Satisfying Explanation
item.description:
Argument from Various Disabilities

These arguments take the form, "I grant you that you can make machines do all the things you have mentioned but you will never be able to make one to do X." Numerous features X are suggested in this connexion. I offer a selection:

Be kind, resourceful, beautiful, friendly, have initiative, have a sense of humor, tell right from wrong, make mistakes, fall in love, enjoy strawberries and cream, make some one fall in love with it, learn from experience, use words properly, be the subject of its own thought, have as much diversity of behavior as a man, do something really new.

No support is usually offered for these statements.

[...]

The criticisms that we are considering here are often disguised forms of the argument from consciousness. Usually if one maintains that a machine can do one of these things, and describes the kind of method that the machine could use, one will not make much of an impression. It is thought that the method (whatever it may be, for it must be mechanical) is really rather base. (emphasis added)

Today, Scott Aaronson hosted an essay discussion at Inkhaven and selected Turing's classic 1950 paper that defines The Imitation Game. After reading it, I find all our present-day conversations about AI do not feel new, but instead feel old. Turing attempts to diagnose the causes of people's disagreement with his position that one day computers will be able to win the imitation game, and he does such a good job of it that most people talking about AI today are just showing the callowness of their youth. But the bolded line felt true and yet I didn't fully grok it, so now I want to understand it better.

What is going on here, with this "base" property? Why does it lead people to false conclusions, that computers cannot do things that humans can? If no longer in-principle, I feel this comes up at least as commonly in-practice in discussion of the limitations of LLMs.

A Millennium Prize problem fell, Navier-Stokes, but it was disproof by counterexample, and thousands of agents explored many different approaches. It is something like simulating hundreds of people working for hundreds of years. This felt to some like creativity was being replaced with brute force.

Related to cool things being made from base mechanisms, I am reminded of this passage by Paul Graham:

Since fundraising appears to be the measure of success for startups (another classic noob mistake), they always want to know what the tricks are for convincing investors. We tell them the best way to convince investors is to make a startup that's actually doing well, meaning growing fast, and then simply tell investors so. Then they want to know what the tricks are for growing fast. And we have to tell them the best way to do that is simply to make something people want.

So many of the conversations YC partners have with young founders begin with the founder asking "How do we..." and the partner replying "Just..."

People often think that fundraising is a prestigious activity, and can be surprised when it's "just" sending emails and having meetings. Graham goes on to write "Startups are as impersonal as physics", which I think can be applied here: the answers to your questions don't meet the mood with which you sought them.

There can be something deflating about having a grand idea, like creating art, or a mathematical proof, and then it being reduced to a bunch of steps each of which is unglamorous. Dennett spoke of this about the consciousness debate, that people feel it is the height of what is great about humanity, and it is unpleasant for it to be broken down into things like working memory, a visual field, physical sensation, reflection, and so forth.

One more example is a critique of capitalism and modernity. It is a common refrain in the broader media that capitalism has replaced meaningful lives with buying goods, where again the sacred meaning is traded out for the mundane appliances. I recall the following Twitter exchange from 2021.

Chris Powers

125 yrs ago not even the richest person in the world could have:

- air conditioning
- home refrigerator
- a flashlight
- a personal computer
- access to an airplane
- a radio
- a television

The world is getting better if you choose to look at progress rather than the media.

QC

none of these things is a substitute for a functional social fabric

it boggles my mind that someone could list a bunch of appliances and consider this a knockdown argument that people’s lives are better now than before. you really think life is about having *appliances*?

[deleted tweet by Sarah Constantin. IIRC it said that they kinda think life is about having appliances]

Divia Eden

Yeah, I kind of do too.

Sarah Cone

Strongly agree! (Also, indicative of how only women seem to feel passionate about this.)

QC

i genuinely did not expect this and i am very curious about it

bosco selene

appliances free up so. much. labor.

my grandmother did washing by hand when she was a kid (v poor) and I remember her telling me I should literally thank Jesus for washing machines

This is an example of something sacred and rich ("a functional social fabric") being determined by something mundane and boring ("appliances"), and thus feeling entirely unsatisfying.

It is interesting that we often find the truth... unsatisfactory. We expected to feel a certain way when we hear the truth, and so it doesn't ring as true to us when we don't feel that way.

As a child, I used to expect that knowing the truth would make me feel safe. Children feel a lot of fear, and often knowing things meant I could push away certain social fears (e.g. fears from teachers). As an adult I don't expect to feel safe with any particular certainty. And I have stopped expecting to feel safe when I have arrived at true conclusions. (On the contrary, I think the truth is regularly somewhat destabilizing, due to reality itself not being very kind to humans.)

The consciousness debate is often one about the very essence of what makes humanity more than mere matter, mere instinctual creatures. I suspect a key reason that people are so resistant to physicalist and functionalist theories is that they wish for them to feel the way they feel about humanity as a whole: a little more magical. Many people attracted to the conversation are attracted substantially for this reason.

In this paper Turing is noticing that many people come to the question of whether a computer can imitate a human out of a desire to ask whether a computer can reach up to the glory and wonder of humankind. But when the details of the answer are mundane—or, to borrow a Dennett-ism, when the glory is built from something that is not itself glorious—this does not satisfy the emotion that brought them to the question, leading them to keep searching for an answer that does, even after they've heard the correct one.

As I read Turing's paper, my attention was repeatedly drawn to how different parts of it matched today's AI conversations. It helped me see the present more clearly, and I see now one reason why people may be resistant to believing that an AI could replace humanity. Part of them feels that humanity is a grand thing, and therefore the AI should be a grand thing. However, while engineers sought to use human ingenuity to design better AIs, they bitterly learned that what works is "just scaling"; and while the world sought stories like The Terminator, the realistic takeover stories are full of mundane details about export controls, job automation, and compute budgets.

Returning to Turing's line:

It is thought that the method (whatever it may be, for it must be mechanical) is really rather base.

Instead of humanity discovering a grand theory of intelligence, intelligence emerges from a dumb machine "just predicting the next word".

As if that could do anything as grand as thinking.

item.title: From epistemic innocence to sophisticated uncertainty
item.description:
When I was young I knew I didn't want to be a political ideologue like my parents. But it seemed to me that that's just what adults were like, and I was protected only by my innocence. Just as I was already beginning to make myself ridiculous acting on newly acquired sexual urges, perhaps becoming overconfident of grand narratives was just part of growing up?

Now I have acquired an ideology (transhumanist, for one thing). And my ideology does come with convenient narratives. Yet, if you'll let me flatter myself, I have not acquired an ideologue's overconfidence.

I did not protect my epistemic innocence. I enjoy seeing the world from a new worldview, including an ideologically charged one. But the result of such openness was that I became familiar with a variety of possibilities with different implications.

Example: nuclear power

In my subculture of tech enthusiasts, you'll hear that the world was ready to transition to nuclear power in the '70s, in which case we would have avoided global warming. However, this technological revolution was stopped by the anti-nuclear movement and burdensome safety regulation.

Probably at some point I was caught up in this narrative. But because I was interested in energy, I read widely, and got caught up in other narratives. That nuclear could not provide return on investment when electricity use was lower than forecasted, and natural gas plants could be built with cheap equipment and surprisingly abundant fuel.

Now I don't know what would have happened had nuclear been allowed to expand and develop. But I am not back in my state of epistemic innocence, before I had any knowledge or opinions on the matter at all. Instead, I know that overregulation was important, and so was gas, and so was weak electricity demand growth. These could have all been equally important, or one could be dominant and make the others negligible. I am uncertain about the counterfactual because I know of multiple possibilities with different predictions.

Sophisticated uncertainty

Sophisticated uncertainty is uncertainty about what a system will do (or would have done), resulting from an ensemble of explicit possibilities for how the system works.

In a state of epistemic innocence, I may have said: "the probability is 50% because it can happen or not". If I have achieved sophisticated uncertainty, I can say: "the probability is 50% because there's these ten ways this could work, and it happens in five of them".

Avoiding overconfidence

The good news I could deliver to my younger self is that overconfidence is not the inevitable or even the natural consequence of sophistication. I am not protected from overconfidence by a skeptic's shield, demanding randomized controlled trials before I consider a possibility. In fact I tend to get carried away by a narrative, and temporarily see everything from its perspective. But when the honeymoon is over, I am not loyal: I'm ready to let it happen again.

Maybe there is a rule to follow here, the one Epicurus articulated in his letter to Pythocles. He said a plausible explanation should never be rejected as long as it is consistent with visible appearances.

One characteristic of a political ideologue is rejecting an explanation for reasons that have nothing to do with its fit to the facts. Because it is flattering to the wrong people, or it undermines an important call to action. You just don't have to do this.

item.title: Moderately cursed questions of AI safety
item.description:
TL;DR

  • AI safety has many moderately cursed questions (as opposed to the extremely cursed questions of s-risk, which we don’t discuss here).
  • Taboo prevents open discussion of these cursed questions in AI safety spaces outside LessWrong.
  • When cursed questions are left unasked, everyone stays confused or reaches private conclusions alone.
  • Spreading decoupling norms, so that cursed questions can be discussed more openly, should be an explicit target of AI safety acculturation.

You’re having Thai food with your fiancée. The wedding is two months out, and you can’t slurp your green curry with the usual gusto. That cursed question keeps buzzing around your head like a hungry fly after your crispy tofu. You’ve been rehearsing ways to broach the subject:

“I was thinking, maybe we should get a prenup? I don’t think anything will happen, it’s just…”

Not that. Might as well say, “You’re cool, but my lawyer told me not to trust you.”

The prenup question is wrapped in taboo. Asking for one feels like pre-filing divorce papers. Yet even while the words stay unspoken, the thought can’t be undone. Unasked questions still exist, just internally.

AI safety has its own cursed questions. In this essay, I discuss four:

  1. Are we better off with a catastrophe big enough to summon the political will to pause AI, but small enough that we survive?
  2. Should AI safety proponents prepare to win a culture war via AI superpersuasion?
  3. Will there come a time when stopping the AI race is infeasible and we must pick a horse?
  4. When do we stop working on AI safety and make end-of-life arrangements?

I. Waiting for Chernobyl

In 1986, Chernobyl exploded. The next year, Italy voted against nuclear energy. The global nuclear construction boom never recovered. In 2010, Germany extended the lifetimes of its reactors but reversed course after the Fukushima disaster months later. Whatever you make of these choices, disaster is a political accelerant like no other.

AI progress has had its warning shots. After the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI paused RL for two weeks and strengthened safety protocols. Yet much AI safety work makes such incidents smaller and rarer. Monitors catch accidents before they become public disasters. Prosaic alignment may hide misbehavior without curing it. We might be removing the warnings, not the x-risk.

If you say you want a warning shot, people may question your intentions, and if disaster comes, they may blame you for encouraging it. Genuine accidents could look like sabotage. But even when unspoken, the question remains:

Is the best-case scenario an AI Chernobyl: a catastrophe big enough to summon the political will to pause AI but small enough that we survive? Or is it continued, apparently safe progress—and whatever comes after?

II. Wars of influence

In 2025, University of Zurich researchers revealed that they had deployed AI bots with fake personas to debate people on r/changemyview. The bots were far more persuasive than human redditors. The troubling implication is that, as we near superintelligence, our opponents will gain superhuman powers of manipulation.

Persuasiveness has never been a good proxy for truth. Scott Alexander illustrates the power of good (human) documentary-makers:

The National Institute of Health can make an engaging human interest documentary about a smoker who got lung cancer. And the tobacco companies can make an engaging human interest documentary about a guy who got cancer because of asbestos, then was saved by tobacco-sponsored research. Opponents of Brexit can make an engaging documentary about all the reasons Brexit would be bad, and then proponents of Brexit can make an engaging documentary about all the reasons Brexit would be good. If you get good documentary-makers, I assume both will be equally convincing regardless of what the true facts are.

Now replace “documentary-makers” with “future AIs,” and multiply the effect by [insert_big_number]. Uh-oh.

Should AI safety proponents prepare to win a culture war via superpersuasion? Must we use AI to win the public argument before others destroy our cause? This could mean making true arguments more accessible. It could also mean manipulating people into supporting policies they wouldn’t otherwise endorse.

Recently, both sides of the AI debate have been churning out AI Doompop videos via Suno and Opus 5.5. Should we gallop into this arms race?

III. Picking a horse

Joseph Rotblat was a physicist who worked on the Manhattan Project. At first, he resisted building the bomb. In his words:

I had this dilemma: on the one hand, as a scientist, I felt it’s against the ideals of science to work on a bomb; on the other hand, the ideals of science were endangered if Hitler and his philosophy of Nazism were to prevail. So I fought with myself throughout the summer of 1939, this dilemma. By that time I already was in England, and I remember, ‘What should I do? Should I begin to work or not?’ Eventually the decision was made for me by the outbreak of the war in September 1939, and immediately my country was overrun at the time, and I see the great might, the military might of Germany, and I felt the immediate crisis should take precedence. So therefore I decided, at that stage, that we ought to work on the bomb.

Rotblat feared the Nazis would build the bomb first. He chose “the good side” over no side at all. Once it was clear Germany had given up on nukes, he quit. The Trinity test happened seven months later.

Will there come a time when stopping the AI race is infeasible and we must pick a horse, as Rotblat did? Each AI lab argues, “The race is inevitable, so help us win.” The frontrunner says, “Help us widen the gap, so that we have room to breathe and focus on safety.”

Will one of them ever be right?

IV. Bunkers and Lambos

“What would you do in a zombie apocalypse?”

Idealists would build a resistance or work on a cure. But when these avenues reach dead ends, they join the pessimists: Gather food. Stock firewood. Build a bunker.

“What would you do if you had one month to live?”

One person says they’d curl up in bed and cry. Another would spew their musings on life into a long letter addressed to no one. Others would go home to their families, tick off bucket-list items, or gorge themselves on Korean barbecue. A few would go shopping for Lamborghinis.

Vishal Prasad says: Silence, Doomchud.

I’m so sick of doomchudding. I agree with you that the probability of ASI doing omnicide is high. So what? That does not mean I welcome having my dinner ruined listening to you mope about how you’ll never have kids. If a planet-killer asteroid were to hit Earth tomorrow, I’d expect you to not go out of your way to ruin my mood today—indeed, I’d appreciate it if you even exhibited some courage in the face of danger. [...] From the war-poems of Wilfred Owen to the Bhagavad Gita, from Hamlet to The Leopard, there are thousands of stories available to you about death, and the death of civilizations. Go read those and let me eat in peace.

If you want to spend your last year alive in an orgiastic fervor, go ahead. Just don’t be a sadsack about it. Spread some joie de vivre while you’re at it. Wouldn’t that be more defiant?

Which, you know, if chasing the Kierkegaardian picturesque staves off the abyss for you, more power to you. But I’ve had a surprisingly difficult time curing people’s AI depression by sneering at their cowardice. Most doomers outside the rationalist bubble are graduating from “Should I apply to a PhD program?” to “How many months of canned food should I hoard?”

Alignment research and AI pause advocacy are the two bets made in the light; many more are made in the shadows. I know plenty of people, recently doom-pilled, who have retreated into those shadows. Whether they go through the motions or quiet-quit, panic-attack or find Jesus, disaster-prep or bucket-list, they are the dark matter of the doomer world. We should address their cursed questions with grace, not sneers.

Lifting the curse

In 2011, a web developer named Jon Underwood wanted a space where people could talk openly about death. He invited a few strangers to his house in London and fed them tea and cake as they discussed dying. The first “Death Café” was born. The concept took off, and there have since been over 25,000 Death Cafés in 100 countries. There is even a website.

AI safety has no Death Cafés outside Berkeley, CA. Instead, it has seminars, where we talk about respectable topics like activation steering and scalable oversight. Then there are the lunch meetings with close friends. We look left and right, lower our voices like children in church, and ask, What do you really think? Is RSI coming in 2027? Should I go all in on ANT?

Not long ago, AI x-risk was itself a cursed question. Skeptics in the early 2010s did not believe deep learning would take off. In the late 2010s, they doubted AI would generalize across tasks. In the early 2020s, they assumed models would not develop long-horizon goals. Afraid of ridicule, worried researchers learned to either keep quiet or camouflage their real concerns in talk of “long-term impacts.”

In May 2023, the Center for AI Safety published a statement declaring that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. Hundreds of researchers and executives signed. Many may have feared making such a bold claim alone; signing alongside hundreds of others was safer. Earlier that month, Geoffrey Hinton left Google to “talk about the dangers of AI without considering how this impacts Google.” His reputation was great enough to withstand whatever backlash followed. Most others could only sign a document; still, AI risk was leaving the lunch table.

Three years later, this tweet from Jacob Coxon got 175 million views:

And then this happened:

Jacob Coxon soon went on CNN and The Daily Show to talk about x-risk. AI safety was thrust into the public imagination, and other researchers felt safer sharing their worries. The credit doesn’t belong to Coxon and Evan Hubinger alone, just as Franz Ferdinand’s assassination did not single-handedly cause WWI. The public had long felt uneasy about automated coding, AI discoveries, and trillion-dollar valuations. Over the years, thousands of advocates turned that private unease into public discourse, and the Overton window moved. AI x-risk has won its right to be discussed. Many of its subquestions have not.

These questions are social dark matter, the things that many of us think about but few discuss openly. Public silence creates a veneer of consensus that masks our deep collective unease.

Sometimes, people like Geoffrey Hinton and Jacob Coxon break the silence. So does Eliezer Yudkowsky’s Only Law Can Prevent Extinction, which addresses the cursed question, “When should AI safety advocates resort to vigilante violence?”

Answer: never.

This was obvious to some and news to others. Without Yudkowsky’s post, each of us would have answered the question alone, through the lens of our own biases.

Yudkowsky has a history of discussing cursed questions. People are not surprised when he answers a new one, so he can share valuable thoughts at little social cost. But many of the others who ask cursed questions are extremists who don’t hesitate to voice toxic opinions. These people tarnish the questions with their own disagreeableness. Taboo selects for a topic’s most unabashed advocates, who in turn make it more taboo.

I don’t know the answers to my cursed questions, but I want us all to be able to ask them openly.

Too often, we fear that our questions will be heard as confessions and that we will be crucified just for asking. Mention a prenup, and your fiancée hears, “Our marriage will crash and burn.” This is the nature of cursed questions. Their dark matter distorts perception.

Astronomers cannot see dark matter, but they know it bends light, and they account for it. So must a good listener. Words are not always what they first feel like. A question is not an endorsement of the vilest answer. An argument for X does not mean the arguer wants X. We should explicitly teach these decoupling norms to AI safety newcomers.

Taboos can take decades to fade. AI progress will not wait that long. How quickly we can clear the dark matter may determine whether we get to make hard choices before it is too late.

item.title: Green = Life - Rectangle
item.description:
Imagine a 2D plane with x- and y-axes labelled “tasty” and “American” respectively. Now, plot the whole space of possible foods, from linguine to Panda Express, along these axes.

This is what LLM representation spaces are like, except instead of projecting foods onto two dimensions, they fit every concept ever into 40,000.

The Linear Representation Hypothesis states that high-level concepts that emerge through training are represented as consistent directions inside the representation space of an LLM. The classic example is king−man+woman ≈ queen, suggesting the existence of a single direction vector that represents the concept of gender.

In the spirit of the Linear Representation Hypothesis, this essay proposes the following equation:

Green = Life - Rectangle

Let’s begin with the definition of Rectangle.

Rectangle

This essay is inspired by the following meme:

By way of example, here are some rectangles:

I was first exposed to rectangles by Book Review: Seeing Like A State. Scott A. (summarizing J. Scott) describes the evolution of scientific forestry practices in 18th-century Prussia:

Enlightenment rationalists noticed that peasants were just cutting down whatever trees happened to grow in the forests, like a chump. They came up with a better idea: clear all the forests and replace them by planting identical copies of Norway spruce (the highest-lumber-yield-per-unit-time tree) in an evenly-spaced rectangular grid. Then you could just walk in with an axe one day and chop down like a zillion trees an hour and have more timber than you could possibly ever want.

It turns out that replacing all the forests with a rectangular tiling of one tree is a terrible, horrible, no-good, very bad, disastrous idea, and the economy went up in flames.

The ecological collapse of the Norway spruce forests is one stark example of a bigger pattern. Large human societies are messy (citation needed), and so the state organizes them into rectangles—city streets, paperwork, farming plots, etc.—in an effort to make these systems legible.

Importantly, not all rectangles cause fiery train wrecks! At a fundamental level, the scale of modern society seems to require them. Rectangles tile the plane perfectly. Rectangles are easy to mass-produce. Rectangles are flexible in a narrow way—you can build larger rectangles of all shapes and sizes out of them. In many ways, the rectangles girding our existence really do protect us from ourselves and from each other.

Architect Christopher Alexander’s A City is Not a Tree is a more abstract screed against rectangles. In C. Alexander’s usage, a tree (in the poset sense) is a poset whose Hasse diagram is a tree (in the graph sense).

In other words, a collection of objects, organized into subsets, is a tree if and only if these subsets can be delineated by nonintersecting rectangles. Real trees tend not to look like rectangles, but poset trees are made up entirely of them.

Modern planned cities are the epitome of poset trees: the city is cut into boroughs, into blocks, into buildings, into floors, each compartment neatly siloed from its neighbors.

Old, organic cities do not look like poset trees because they have had time to grow and interconnect naturally. For instance, the streets of Boston seem laid out by the insane:

I worry that I am making it sound like rectangles just sort of manifested out of authoritarian will. Like one day we all woke up and fascistly decided that ellipsoids were out and right angles were in.

That is not what happened.

In A City is Not a Tree, C. Alexander lays the blame for the rectangularization of the modern city at the feet of human psychology:

It is known today that grouping and categorization are among the most primitive psychological processes. Modern psychology treats thought as a process of fitting new situations into existing slots and pigeonholes in the mind. Just as you cannot put a physical thing into more than one physical pigeonhole at once, so, by analogy, the processes of thought prevent you from putting a mental construct into more than one mental category at once.

Forget about Big Brother: it’s the iron fist of Marie Kondo in each of us that needs to pack all of reality into shapes with four right angles. The word rectify, meaning “to correct”, derives from the Latin rectificare (“to make right or straight”). This psychological vision explains the onset of modernity not as a grand unifying project, but rather as giving in to the giddy child with Legos inside all of us who just really, really loves packing things into neat little boxes.

Rectangles are also a particular approach to optimization. They are the Order of the paperclip-maximizing fae who ask for the Tower of Babel to be built just one story higher.

Most (modern) buildings are rectangles: subway stations, warehouses, garages, strip malls, schools, etc. Almost all of these rectangular buildings exist in an attempt to optimize some value in the world—square footage into sleepspace, travel times through cityspace, writing time in bureaucracyspace. (This is not solely a phenomenon of the Industrial Revolution or modernity. The whole thesis of J. Scott’s later book about ancient civilizations can be summed up as: wheat is a rectangle.)

Seeing Like a State frames the rectifying of the world as a progressive story. When Le Corbusier, one of the fathers of modern architecture, traveling-salesmanned around Europe shopping his vision of a mega-super-rectangle-world, his was a progressive, revolutionary endeavor.

But I think the proliferation of rectangles in our civilization is more than just progressive overreach. Its psychological history is also touched by a unique flavor of anxiety and conservatism.

Rectangles are neatness, order, and clean boundaries. (I am reminded of Scott Alexander’s A Thrive/Survive Theory of the Political Spectrum and how conservatism seems to be more popular in countries wracked by disease.) We want hospital cleanrooms to be tiled with squeaky-clean rectangles. Similarly, the zombie apocalypse will be filled with rectangles: fortresses, sterile chambers, warehouse stockpiles, underground bunkers.

The spirit of rectangles is the style of engineering that says: safety is putting as many rectangles as possible between human life and nature.

Green

Duncan Sabien’s classic The MTG Color Wheel (& Humanity) identifies five philosophical approaches towards life with the five colors of the Magic: The Gathering color wheel:

Drawn from the in-game mechanics and decades of flavor text, each color represents a philosophy that is, in Sabien’s words, “a near-enough-to-be-thought-provoking match for reality.”

Of the five colors, Blue (perfection through knowledge) fits rationalists like a glove, while Green (harmony through acceptance) remains the least understood.

Green is the patient, passive, fertile interconnectedness of organic plant life. Biological cells are Green: all the chemicals are mixed haphazardly inside and left to chance and the law of large numbers.

Model of a Mycoplasma cell.

Green has a nonintegral fractal dimension.

Green is the richly interconnected map of Dark Souls 2, as well as its gender-affirming coffin.

Fundamentally, Green systems are ones with many internally conflicting values/parts that have reached equilibrium via natural selection, Wikipedia edit wars, or spontaneous divine grace.

Green can be big (in MTG, we call this archetype “big stompy”). But it isn’t about size so much as age. Green embraces how ecosystems become messy and interconnected over time.

Green is also a way of doing things. Joe Carlsmith describes Green-as-a-verb in On attunement:

Whatever our meta-ethics, we can agree that there is a thing that humans do, when they turn outwards, and with their hearts open; seeking, in yin, some truer contact with the good; trying to listen more deeply to the great song of the world. And we can agree that this thing, and the thing-it-discloses when done well, is profoundly precious.

For Carlsmith, attunement is about opening yourself up to the world. We spend so much of our lives narrowing our attention: to the physical work we do, to the things we see and hear, to the people around us, to what we believe in.

Attunement is about widening our attention to all aspects of the world—the smell of fallen leaves, the surrounding buildings that breach the sky, the 250k-page AI proof of the Riemann Hypothesis—and letting them wash over us, all at the same time.

Green is pulling numbers out of your ass to feed to Bayes’ theorem. Green is attuning your bodily senses to your vast subconscious via Gendlin’s Focusing (for AI researchers, this is training your body to be a natural language autoencoder). Green is about ritual, wisdom, history; it’s about how sometimes you step outside in the morning and you just get it. You look up at the sun and feel you are a thread in the continuous tapestry that ties together the disparate pieces of this strange and fragile world we find ourselves in.

It does not work this way all of the time.

Most of the time, when I step outside in the morning, I am already thinking about someone I need to text and when Claude is going to finish the last task I gave it and anything other than the fact that I’m here right now. Before I even get a chance to breathe in the air that reeks of weed and poop (good earth smells, as they call them), I am already dreaming of going back inside where my biggest problem is the charging cable not reaching my bed.

I personally care about attunement because I would like more mornings of the first kind rather than the second. But also: I know some people who have largely avoided the modern world, and for a long time, I’ve wanted a word describing their philosophy.

One of them is a retired park ranger who lives in a cabin probably hundreds of miles from the nearest LessWrong lurker. Naturally, I showed her a printout of the MTG color wheel. She told me she was Blue. So I slowly went through and re-explained each of the colors.

“Yep,” she said. “Blue seems right.”

Her job, it turned out, mostly consisted of hitting Ctrl-F for “bear” across 5.89 million acres. The idea was to isolate specific parts of the forest. Despite the superficial connection to Green, Blue fit her better.

Green is not equivalent to nature, and not every part of a Green ecosystem is necessarily Green. After a fire in the western US, lodgepole pines can regrow in the burn scar so quickly that they crowd out everything else. The trees should thin out and die back, and yet they often don’t.

Green has limitations. In its acceptance, it strives too little. In its messiness, it holds back replication and scaling. In its opacity, it can never be perfectly safe and reliable.

To take an extremely simple example that nobody has ever disagreed about, consider the beginning of human civilization. You can get this from Your Book Review: The Dawn of Everything, but this will be approximately 8,592 words shorter:

In early human civilizations, everybody knows everybody else and has complicated and multifaceted relationships with all of them.

It’s all very Green. Imagine explaining to an outsider from within a hunter-gatherer society how the power structure is set up: “So you see, Clara and I agree that hunting elk is bad luck during the dry season, but only because Clara’s mother had a dream about it, and nobody wants to contradict Clara’s mother because she’s the one who knows which mushrooms are fine, except she’s not really in charge either because Tomas once carried her brother, who had broken his leg, three miles from that hill over there, and so now she owes him, but also Tomas…”

This kind of Green society works great until one day you decide you want a civilization with more than, like, you and your friends and the guy down the street.

You can try to sidestep our hardwired limits on relationships, but while social media increases our raw numerical capacity for relationships, it also flattens and uniformizes them. LinkedIn is decidedly not Green. At some point, once you have enough people kicking around in the same place, you start building rectangles.

The Human in the Rectangle

Green and Rectangle have been locked in primordial battle since probably forever. Green is a Slavic wrestler who is impossible to knock over and has been incubating in a UFC-octagon-sized vat since the age of four.

Rectangle sees messy cowpaths stretching out across a city and goes, “It’s pavement time.” And then Green shows up and patiently crunches through those sidewalk tiles.

On a grander scale: most buildings are rectangles, but most religious architecture is not.

Look at all those arches.

The High Line in New York is one of my favorite places to walk: it cuts through the poset-tree boundaries of the city, meandering through many different communities along elevated pathways that disrupt the street grid.

Duncan Sabien recently wrote an essay, You are the Deer in the Subway. He doesn’t use these words, but in his formulation, humans are the battleground on which the fight between Green and Rectangle plays out.

Back when Dunbar’s number was the cool kid on the block running human civilization, humans were connected to everything: we were constantly being touched by the world, by the water, by animals, and by each other. One by one by one, we packed these things away into tidy rectangles.

We let our rectifying neuroticism go too far. We pruned away extended families and intergenerational friendships and replaced them with atomized individualism.

We built pocket rectangles to summon human connection, but like a demon that wears its summoner’s skin, the pocket rectangle now gets more of our touch than the humans it summons.

We cut the woods down and replaced them with acres of wimpy lawn grass and then refused to touch such grass.

When you grow a tree in too small a container, its roots wrap around the tree itself, strangling it.

The deer does not belong among the rectangles. The deer belongs in the Green. The deer is you.

The Green in the Machine

Recently, the phrase “AIs are grown, not built,” popularized by Soares and Yudkowsky, has captured the public imagination. The phrase is so compelling because it points to the central conceptual tension of modern LLMs.

In one sense, modern LLMs are the pinnacle of Rectangle. They are rectangles:

…living in rectangles…

…packed into rectangles…

…housed in the biggest rectangles ever built by human civilization.

And yet, LLMs are grown, not built, in a fundamentally MTG-Green way.

Attention is the sole ingredient of attunement. In a transformer, at every layer, every token can pull directly from any earlier token. LLM attention flows freely and winds up with bizarre and idiosyncratic habits. LLMs spend a lot of time staring blankly into the void.

Polysemanticity and superposition are Green, mirroring pleiotropy in human genetics. A single neuron can fire on academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests, and Korean text.

Many image models produce uncanny outputs in which every pixel overflows with detail. These images are unsettling precisely because they are less rectangular than the world they seek to reflect, and tend towards the same nonintegral fractal dimension typified by Green:

Somehow, in the most rectangular of rectangles, we’ve grown the most organic Green entities ever to exist in silico. Life finds a way.

In Foundation, Asimov envisions the ultimate sci-fi world as a planet completely paved over with concrete rectangles. It is the neurotic, platonic ideal of the city-tree (to use C. Alexander’s term).

It is no crime to approach one color with another, but these visions of rectangular futures arise from ingrained misconceptions about AI. We’ve painted machines with an impoverished Blue-White color palette for so long that we can’t see Green when it stares us in the face.

Interpretability seems like a Blue-White stance towards fighting the fundamental Greenness of LLMs. Sparse autoencoders attempt to extract single functions out of the root system, but the living roots resist. If you cut out a circuit, the model regrows it elsewhere. We quest for monosemanticity and it goes, uh, not well.

(Bonsai is the best recent example of boxing Green into a tiny rectangle. Bonsai is a 1-bit LLM that you can probably run on your own computer, poking at its neurons yourself. Completely unrelatedly, when most real bonsai trees die, you don’t notice until well after it’s too late.)

The goal seems to be to stifle the Green creeping into the machine and cage it in increasingly neat rectangles. I suspect there’s room for more congruous in-color approaches to AI safety.

If Blue-White rectification is the approach of scientists and engineers, then a Green approach smells more like druidry, in the spirit of Anna Salamon’s Takes from two months as an aspiring LLM naturalist. For roughly the same reason rationalists crave spirituality, I think we need more AI safety druids.

I plan to elaborate on AI druidry in an upcoming post, but the fundamental principle of druidry is for the pre-verbal Green parts of your brain to communicate with the Green in the machine.

item.title: Banana Cases
item.description:
Ages ago I saw some banana cases in the grocery store. They seemed like a gimmick: why would you get a piece of plastic for such a specific use? A decade later we have a set of three and use them ~daily.

Nora (5y) really likes bananas, and is now in kindergarten. She wants to bring them to school, which is great: they're tasty, reasonably healthy, and very cheap.

(I do want to stop for a minute and gush about how through shipping and ethylene gas management my 5yo can eat tropical fruit all through the New England winter. World banana production is not perfect, but it is pretty incredible.)

Initially I was putting them in the same random set of containers we use for storing non-hot leftovers. These either were too small for a banana or took up too much space in her lunchbox. They also sealed too well, and so let the ethylene build up and accelerate ripening. I remembered the banana cases, sized for a banana with vent holes for gas exchange, and decided to get some (3 for $8).

They work well, and the bananas don't squish. I do sometimes need to cut off the stem for them to fit, and need to avoid unusually large bananas. Still, I was unreasonably dismissive of these: they solve a real problem, and they do it well.

item.title: Announcing RLLW: Reinforcement Learning via LessWrong
item.description:
You’ve railed against RLHF.

My job was stolen by RLVR.

Welcome to RLLW.

I think LessWrong and the blogosphere around it host the most important public conversations in the world, and there aren’t enough dedicated writers to produce the long-form content about rationality and AI we all crave. RLLW is my attempt to train a few. In the first cohort, I am working with two undergraduate apprentices, who will each write one post every two weeks.

Sam Worthington: Sam goes to Princeton and co-directs Princeton AI Alignment. He hopes to maximize his EV by getting himself into increasing amounts of trouble. He also writes here.

Jaisen Soundar: Jaisen goes to Georgia Tech and does technical AI safety research. He hopes to make a positive impact on the field through his writing.

The first round of essays

  1. Green = Life − Rectangle (Sam) asks what’s up with all these rectangles everywhere and why AIs don’t seem to fit in them.
  2. Moderately cursed questions of AI safety (Jaisen) Explores four questions in AI safety that people think about but rarely discuss openly.

Philosophy: Microdosing the Spirit of Inkhaven

I had planned to frame this announcement as an answer to Ben Pace’s call for better writing on LessWrong, but that call was unfortunately rebutted soundly by Ben Pace.

In this section I ramble about a couple of different things I’m trying, especially in contrast to Inkhaven. We’ll post once every two weeks for two months instead of every day for a month. More details:

  • Each two-week sprint is broken into a Babble week and a Prune week.
  • Iterated Distillation and Amplification is a useful frame for skilling up on writing. Amplify by spending a lot more time perfecting pieces; distill/quantize to produce quality work more quickly once you’ve trained your taste to the next level. Inkhaven is mostly a distillation cycle for training a Flash model of yourself. Newbie writers should start with an amplification cycle.
  • Writing practice is mostly compound exercises, and I’ll try to inject isolation exercises. Every Prune week will have a main focus, like Omit Needless Words or Microhumor.
  • Cowriting is a clumsy beast, and LW dialogues never quite took off. I am trying out a new model, importing the technology of writing math papers with my graduate students: I provide a fuzzy vision of the final piece, they write the thing, I keep polishing until it’s to my liking.
  • We write in a “composite first person”: the authorial “I” refers to either or both authors, as convenient. This is useful because writing is mostly mining one’s own experience, and the composite “I” has twice as many experiences to mine. And because I have to take only half responsibility for all my cringe takes.

Please read the essays!
